stem: Before the first dose of a newly prescribed CNS stimulant, a nurse discovers a documented cardiac arrhythmia that may not have been considered when the prescription was written. What is the safest action?

options.A: Administer the dose because stimulants improve cardiac function
options.B: Ignore the history because stimulants do not affect heart rate or blood pressure
options.C: Permanently stop all future ADHD treatment because any past arrhythmia is an absolute contraindication
options.D: Clarify the cardiac history and prescription with the prescriber before administration

rationale: Current methylphenidate labeling warns against use in patients with serious cardiac disease, including serious cardiac arrhythmia, and states that CNS stimulants increase blood pressure and heart rate. A newly identified arrhythmia therefore requires prescriber clarification and individualized assessment before the first dose. The label does not make every past arrhythmia an automatic permanent contraindication to all ADHD treatment. D is correct.
educational_objective: Identify when a cardiac history requires clarification before initiating stimulant therapy.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine (official FDA drug labeling)
source_locator: Warnings and Precautions 5.2 Risks to Patients with Serious Cardiac Disease; 5.3 Increased Blood Pressure and Heart Rate
source_claim_supported: CNS stimulants can increase blood pressure and heart rate; methylphenidate labeling advises avoiding use in serious cardiac disease including serious cardiac arrhythmia.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication administration, contraindications/precautions, and monitoring
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — stimulant cardiac safety

source_original.stem: A nurse reviews a new stimulant prescription for a client with a documented cardiac arrhythmia that the prescriber may not have considered. What is the safest nursing response?

options.A: Assume stimulant therapy improves cardiac function and give the first dose without further review
options.B: Ignore the cardiac history because stimulants do not affect heart rate or systemic blood pressure
options.C: Hold all future ADHD therapy permanently because any past arrhythmia is an absolute contraindication
options.D: Clarify the cardiac history with the prescriber because stimulants can raise heart rate and blood pressure

source_original.rationale: CNS stimulants can increase heart rate and blood pressure, and product labeling warns against use in serious cardiac disease. A documented arrhythmia warrants prescriber review and individualized risk assessment; a mild past arrhythmia is not automatically an absolute contraindication.
source_original.source_detail: CNS stimulant labeling: increased blood pressure/heart rate and warnings in serious cardiac disease; reviewed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the generic FDA label directory with a current product-specific DailyMed label and narrowed the safety claim to serious cardiac disease/serious cardiac arrhythmia. Final action is prescriber clarification before first dose; difficulty reduced from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current official DailyMed methylphenidate label; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.claim_audit: Serious cardiac arrhythmia is included in the serious-cardiac-disease warning and stimulants increase heart rate and blood pressure.

distractor_audit.A: Stimulants are not given to improve cardiac function.
distractor_audit.C: Overstates the label; not every past arrhythmia permanently excludes all ADHD therapy.
distractor_audit.D: Safest because an unreviewed cardiac risk requires clarification before administration.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: D is the only action that addresses the newly discovered potentially relevant risk without inventing a universal contraindication.
audit_findings.cueing: Removed explanatory clause from the keyed option; the rationale carries the pharmacology.
audit_findings.blueprint: Medication precautions and pre-administration safety fit Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked sections 5.2 and 5.3; D remains uniquely defensible.
